name: Otto Wagner
bio: Wagner spent his first decades building competent Ringstrasse historicism, then, past fifty, publicly renounced it: his 1895 textbook Moderne Architektur told students that only what is practical can be beautiful, and the necessities of modern life — not the styles of dead ones — should generate form. As professor at the Vienna Academy and chief architect of the city's new Stadtbahn, he had the platform and the commissions to prove it, cladding stations, bridges and apartment blocks in a language of marble panels, aluminum bolts and sunflower ornament that hovered exactly between the Secession and the century to come. The Postal Savings Bank, its banking hall lit through a glass ceiling and warmed by aluminum blast heaters, is functionalism before the word existed. His church at the Steinhof asylum gave psychiatric patients a gilded dome and shortened pews with rounded edges. He died in 1918 with the empire he had rebuilt in modern dress, having taught half of Central Europe's next generation — Plečnik, Hoffmann and Olbrich among them.

projects.title: Austrian Postal Savings Bank
projects.blurb: Marble slabs bolted visibly to the facade and a glass-vaulted banking hall — the building that made construction itself the ornament.

projects.title: Kirche am Steinhof
projects.blurb: A white-and-gold domed church for a psychiatric hospital, engineered for hygiene, sightlines and dignity in equal measure.

projects.title: Vienna Stadtbahn
projects.blurb: Stations, viaducts and bridges for the metropolitan railway — infrastructure treated as civic architecture for the first time.

projects.title: Karlsplatz Stadtbahn Pavilions
projects.blurb: Twin station pavilions of steel, marble and gilded sunflowers; the Secession's most reproduced image after Olbrich's dome.

projects.title: Linke Wienzeile Buildings
projects.blurb: Two apartment blocks including the Majolikahaus, its facade a single washable field of flowering ceramic tile.

projects.title: Hofpavillon Hietzing
projects.blurb: A private Stadtbahn station for Emperor Franz Joseph, who used it exactly twice.

projects.title: Nussdorf Weir and Lock
projects.blurb: Danube flood-control infrastructure guarded by bronze lions — engineering given imperial rhetoric.

projects.title: Ankerhaus
projects.blurb: A Graben commercial building with a fully glazed ground floor and a rooftop studio Wagner kept for himself.

projects.title: First Villa Wagner
projects.blurb: His Palladian suburban villa, later sold and now the Ernst Fuchs Museum; the historicist self he would spend a career renouncing.

projects.title: Second Villa Wagner
projects.blurb: The compact late villa next door to the first — asymmetrical, aluminum-trimmed, and a quarter century of theory apart.

name: Antoni Gaudí
bio: A coppersmith's son from Reus, Gaudí took the Catalan Modernisme of his contemporaries and pushed it somewhere structural rather than decorative: he derived his leaning columns and ruled-surface vaults from hanging chain models, weighted with birdshot and photographed upside down, so that his most extravagant forms are also his most rational. The industrialist Eusebi Güell gave him a palace, a park and a workers' colony to experiment on; the Casa Milà gave Barcelona a facade like a cliff face and a roofscape patrolled by helmeted chimneys. In 1883 he took over the Sagrada Família, and from 1914 he worked on nothing else, sleeping on site, dressed so shabbily that when a tram struck him in 1926 he was taken for a beggar and brought to a paupers' ward. Barcelona gave him a state funeral; seven of his works are now World Heritage Sites, and the basilica is still under construction. No architect has ever been less imitable, which has not stopped anyone from trying.

projects.title: Sagrada Família
projects.blurb: The expiatory basilica he served for forty-three years and knowingly left to future generations; a structural system disguised as a vision.

projects.title: Casa Milà
projects.blurb: An apartment block with an undulating limestone facade, no load-bearing walls, and a roof of hooded chimney sentinels — La Pedrera, the quarry.

projects.title: Park Güell
projects.blurb: A failed garden suburb turned public park — viaducts grown from the hillside and the trencadís serpentine bench above the city.

projects.title: Casa Batlló
projects.blurb: A remodel that dissolved a dull apartment house into bone-like columns, a scaled dragon roof and a light well graded from deep to pale blue.

projects.title: Palau Güell
projects.blurb: A dark urban palace organized around a central hall rising into a perforated parabolic dome.

projects.title: Church of Colònia Güell
projects.blurb: Only the crypt was built, but its leaning basalt columns — designed with the hanging model — are the laboratory for everything in the Sagrada Família.

projects.title: Casa Vicens
projects.blurb: His first house, a Moorish-inflected summer villa in checkerboard tile; Modernisme's opening statement.

projects.title: Bellesguard
projects.blurb: A castle-like house in slate and stone on the site of a medieval royal residence, straight lines for once — mostly.

projects.title: Episcopal Palace of Astorga
projects.blurb: A neo-Gothic granite palace for a bishop friend, abandoned mid-build when the bishop died and the chapter balked.

projects.title: El Capricho
projects.blurb: An early villa striped in sunflower tiles for a bachelor indiano, with a minaret-like lookout tower.

name: Louis Sullivan
bio: Sullivan entered MIT at sixteen, lasted a year at the École des Beaux-Arts, and found his real education in the steel frames going up in post-fire Chicago. In partnership with the engineer Dankmar Adler from 1883, he gave the new skyscraper its first coherent artistic form — base, shaft and cornice, with vertical piers pulled taut and his own seething organic ornament poured into the spandrels — and gave the discipline its most misquoted sentence: form ever follows function. The young Frank Lloyd Wright drafted at his elbow and called him Lieber Meister for the rest of his life. After the partnership dissolved in 1895 the commissions thinned to a trickle, and Sullivan spent his last two decades scattering small-town Midwestern banks like jewel boxes across Iowa, Minnesota and Ohio. He died broke in a Chicago hotel room in 1924, days after receiving the first copies of his Autobiography of an Idea.

projects.title: Wainwright Building
projects.blurb: The first skyscraper to look like one on purpose — every vertical line insisting, as Sullivan wrote, that it be tall, every inch of it proud and soaring.

projects.title: Guaranty Building
projects.blurb: The Wainwright idea perfected, wrapped entirely in red terracotta ornament that grows denser as the building rises.

projects.title: Carson Pirie Scott Store
projects.blurb: Wide Chicago windows above and a corner entrance wreathed in cast-iron foliage below; the department store as honest frame plus seduction.

projects.title: Auditorium Building
projects.blurb: Hotel, offices and a 4,000-seat theater with legendary acoustics in one granite mass — Adler & Sullivan's colossal breakthrough.

projects.title: National Farmers' Bank
projects.blurb: The first and grandest of the late jewel-box banks: a brick cube with two great arched windows and an interior of stenciled color.

projects.title: Bayard–Condict Building
projects.blurb: His only New York building, a white terracotta frame crowned with six winged figures.

projects.title: Chicago Stock Exchange Building
projects.blurb: Demolished in 1972 despite protest; the Trading Room was reassembled in the Art Institute, and the fight helped invent American preservation.

projects.title: Merchants' National Bank
projects.blurb: A brick box detonated by one enormous circular ornament over the door.

projects.title: Peoples Federal Savings and Loan
projects.blurb: A late bank still operating as one, its facade carrying a green mosaic panel reading, simply, Thrift.
projects.wikipedia: Peoples Federal Savings and Loan Association

projects.title: Krause Music Store
projects.blurb: His last commission: a single green terracotta facade, the ornament as dense as ever, for a neighborhood music shop.

name: Victor Horta
bio: With the Hôtel Tassel of 1893, Horta did something genuinely without precedent: he took iron — until then the material of stations and greenhouses — into the bourgeois town house, let it show, and bent it into the whiplash line that named a movement. For a decade he was the busiest architect in Brussels, building houses for industrialists, a department store, and the Maison du Peuple for the Socialist party, each one a total design down to the door handles and radiator grilles. He fled to England and America during the First World War and came back a classicist, producing the stripped, coffered Palais des Beaux-Arts as if the whiplash decade had been someone else's. Brussels demolished the Maison du Peuple in 1965 in one of preservation's canonical crimes; four of his surviving town houses, including his own house and studio, are now World Heritage Sites. The style he invented burned out in fifteen years, which he understood better than his imitators did.

projects.title: Hôtel Tassel
projects.blurb: The consensus first building of Art Nouveau — an exposed iron column sprouting painted tendrils up the stairwell of a professor's house.

projects.title: Hôtel Solvay
projects.blurb: An unlimited budget from a chemical dynasty, spent on a facade of bowed stone and an interior where every object is Horta's.

projects.title: Hôtel van Eetvelde
projects.blurb: A town house for the administrator of the Congo Free State, organized around a glass-domed octagonal winter garden — colonial money made uncomfortably visible.

projects.title: Maison & Atelier Horta
projects.blurb: His own house and studio in Saint-Gilles, now the Horta Museum; the staircase ends in a canopy of mirrors and golden glass.

projects.title: Maison du Peuple
projects.blurb: An iron-and-glass headquarters and auditorium for the Belgian Workers' Party, demolished in 1965 over international protest.

projects.title: Magasins Waucquez
projects.blurb: A daylit textile department store, rescued in the 1980s to house the Belgian Comic Strip Center.

projects.title: Palais des Beaux-Arts
projects.blurb: The late classicist Horta: a multi-arts complex buried in a sloping site, now Bozar.

projects.title: Brussels-Central Station
projects.blurb: The junction station he worked on for decades, completed by Maxime Brunfaut after his death.

projects.title: Hôtel Max Hallet
projects.blurb: A late, calmer town house on Avenue Louise for a socialist lawyer; the whiplash line at its most restrained.

projects.title: Hôtel Aubecq
projects.blurb: Demolished in 1949; the numbered stones of its facade sat in storage for decades, a preservation parable.

name: Frank Lloyd Wright
bio: Over a seven-decade career that outlasted every movement it touched, Wright argued that American architecture should grow from its own ground rather than borrow from Europe. The Prairie houses stretched the home into long horizontal planes; the Usonian houses tried to make that vision affordable; Fallingwater and the Guggenheim made it mythic. He worked from Taliesin in Wisconsin and Taliesin West in the Arizona desert, surrounded by an apprentice fellowship that was part school, part farm, and part cult of personality. Arrogant, broke, scandal-prone and endlessly inventive, he remains the figure against whom American architects still measure themselves.

projects.title: Fallingwater
projects.blurb: Cantilevered trays over a waterfall; the most famous house in America.

projects.title: Guggenheim Museum
projects.blurb: A single spiral ramp that made the museum itself the exhibit.

projects.title: Robie House
projects.blurb: The Prairie house at full stretch — hovering roofs and Roman brick.

projects.title: Johnson Wax HQ
projects.blurb: A great room of dendriform columns lit through Pyrex tubing.

projects.title: Taliesin
projects.blurb: His own home, studio and school, rebuilt across a lifetime.

projects.title: Taliesin West
projects.blurb: Desert masonry and canvas roofs; the winter camp that became a campus.

projects.title: Unity Temple
projects.blurb: A monolithic concrete cube for worship — radical for 1908.

projects.title: Hollyhock House
projects.blurb: A Mayan-inflected art-house for an oil heiress; now a UNESCO site.

projects.title: Price Tower
projects.blurb: His only realized skyscraper — a tree that escaped the forest.

projects.title: Marin County Civic Center
projects.blurb: Arched wings striding across the hills, finished after his death.

name: Charles Rennie Mackintosh
bio: A Glasgow policeman's son who won the Glasgow School of Art commission at twenty-eight as a junior in Honeyman & Keppie's office, Mackintosh built almost everything that matters in his catalogue within about fifteen years and within a few miles of the Clyde. With his wife Margaret Macdonald — of whom he said she was half, if not three-quarters, of everything — he fused Scottish baronial mass with an attenuated floral geometry that Vienna adored and London ignored. The Art School's 1909 library, a dark timber cage hung inside a stone cliff, was arguably Britain's first modern interior; it burned in 2014 and again, catastrophically, in 2018 mid-restoration. Passed over at home, he left practice in 1913, drifted to Suffolk and then Port Vendres, and spent his last years painting watercolors of hillsides and flowers. He died in London in 1928, worth almost nothing; Glasgow has been apologizing ever since.

projects.title: Glasgow School of Art
projects.blurb: His masterwork in two campaigns, the second delivering the timber-vaulted library; gutted by fires in 2014 and 2018, its rebuilding still contested.

projects.title: The Hill House
projects.blurb: A publisher's house above the Clyde — baronial outside, white and silver inside; currently drying out inside a chainmail box.

projects.title: Willow Tearooms
projects.blurb: Miss Cranston's Sauchiehall Street tearooms, designed with Margaret down to the cutlery and the waitresses' dresses.

projects.title: Queen's Cross Church
projects.blurb: His only completed church, Gothic massing crossed with Glasgow Style detail; now the Mackintosh Society's home.

projects.title: Scotland Street School
projects.blurb: A board school with two glazed stair towers flooding the halls with light; his last major Glasgow building.

projects.title: 78 Derngate
projects.blurb: A terraced-house remodel for W. J. Bassett-Lowke — black walls and electric geometric friezes that anticipate Art Deco.

projects.title: Windyhill
projects.blurb: The Hill House's rougher elder sibling, a harled family house that stayed private.

projects.title: The Lighthouse
projects.blurb: The Glasgow Herald building with its corner water tower, his first significant work; later Scotland's centre for design and architecture.

projects.title: Martyrs' School
projects.blurb: An early board school near his birthplace, the roof trusses already unmistakably his.

projects.title: House for an Art Lover
projects.blurb: His German competition portfolio built posthumously in Bellahouston Park, ninety-five years late.

name: Adolf Loos
bio: Loos, a Brno stonemason's son who spent three formative years in 1890s America washing dishes and absorbing plumbing, returned to Vienna convinced that his city's beloved ornament was a symptom of cultural backwardness — a thesis he delivered in the 1910 lecture Ornament and Crime, the most quoted polemic in architecture. His buildings practiced a subtler doctrine than the essays preached: plain outside, luxurious inside, with marble, mahogany and brass doing the work that carving used to. The ornament-free Looshaus facing the Hofburg so offended the emperor that he reportedly kept the curtains drawn. Loos's real invention was the Raumplan — rooms of different heights interlocked in section rather than stacked in floors — brought to its finest pitch in Prague's Villa Müller. Nearly deaf, thrice married, disgraced by a 1928 morals trial, he died in 1933 having designed his own grave marker: a plain cube, naturally.

projects.title: Villa Müller
projects.blurb: The Raumplan at full maturity — a white cube outside, a spatial staircase of green marble and lemonwood rooms inside.

projects.title: Looshaus
projects.blurb: The Goldman & Salatsch building on Michaelerplatz: rich Cipollino marble below, famously eyebrow-less windows above, imperial outrage all around.

projects.title: American Bar
projects.blurb: A tiny Kärntner Strasse bar made vast by mirrors, onyx and a coffered marble ceiling; still pouring.

projects.title: Steiner House
projects.blurb: A garden facade of stark white symmetry, endlessly reproduced as proto-modernism — usually cropped to hide the curved street roof.

projects.title: Moller House
projects.blurb: A blank street face with one projecting box; behind it, the Raumplan steps up through the house in half levels.

projects.title: Maison Tristan Tzara
projects.blurb: A Montmartre house for the Dada founder, from Loos's Paris exile among the avant-garde he half despised.

projects.title: Café Museum
projects.blurb: So ostentatiously plain that contemporaries nicknamed it Café Nihilismus; the intelligentsia moved in anyway.

projects.title: Scheu House
projects.blurb: A stepped, flat-roofed terrace house that scandalized Hietzing and anticipated a half century of setbacks.

projects.title: Rufer House
projects.blurb: A near-perfect cube with windows placed only where the interior wanted them; the Raumplan's first full statement.

projects.title: Chicago Tribune Column
projects.blurb: His competition entry: a skyscraper as one colossal Doric column, either the best joke or the most serious proposal in the whole famous field.

name: Jože Plečnik
bio: A carpenter's son from Ljubljana and one of Otto Wagner's favorite students, Plečnik took the master's modern construction and bent it toward something no one else wanted: a personal, almost private classicism, columns and pyramids reassembled with a folk artist's freedom. Vienna gave him the concrete Zacherlhaus; Prague gave him the Castle, which President Masaryk asked him to transform from imperial fortress into the acropolis of a democracy. From 1921 he taught in Ljubljana and quietly rebuilt his home city — bridges, market, library, cemetery, riverbanks — turning a provincial town into a coherent capital on a municipal budget, largely with classical elements he priced like a craftsman. Deeply pious and monastically frugal, he lived in a small house in Trnovo now kept as his museum. Dismissed for decades as a reactionary, he was rediscovered by the postmodernists; UNESCO listed his Ljubljana works in 2021 as a one-man urban vision.

projects.title: National and University Library
projects.blurb: A facade of mingled brick and rough stone, a dark stair rising between polished columns to a luminous reading room: knowledge as ascent.
projects.wikipedia: National and University Library of Slovenia

projects.title: Triple Bridge
projects.blurb: Two pedestrian bridges grafted onto an old road bridge at fanning angles — the hinge of his whole Ljubljana plan.

projects.title: Prague Castle Renovations
projects.blurb: Courtyards, gardens, obelisk and stairways reworked for Masaryk's new republic; a democracy furnished by a Slovene classicist.

projects.title: Church of the Most Sacred Heart of Our Lord
projects.blurb: A great brick vessel in Vinohrady with a slab tower pierced by a giant glass clock face.
projects.wikipedia: Church of the Most Sacred Heart of Our Lord

projects.title: Zacherlhaus
projects.blurb: A granite-clad, concrete-framed apartment block for an insecticide magnate; Wagner-school modernity with a saint on the corner.

projects.title: Žale Cemetery
projects.blurb: A garden of farewell: a monumental entrance arcade and a village of small chapels, one per patron saint, for the city's dead.

projects.title: Ljubljana Central Market
projects.blurb: A colonnaded market hall curving along the river between his bridges, part stoa, part shopfront.

projects.title: Križanke
projects.blurb: A former monastery converted into an open-air theater; his last major work, finished in his eighties.

projects.title: Church of St. Michael
projects.blurb: A marsh church on a shoestring — sewer pipes as columns, timber hall raised on a stone undercroft, bell tower as gate.
projects.wikipedia: Church of St. Michael in the Marsh

projects.title: Ljubljanica Sluice Gate
projects.blurb: A piece of river infrastructure dressed as a temple with three pylons; even the floodgates got columns.

name: Julia Morgan
bio: Morgan took a civil engineering degree at Berkeley, then besieged the École des Beaux-Arts until it admitted her in 1898 as the first woman in its architecture section — reportedly after examiners had marked her down for being one. Back in California she became the state's first licensed woman architect, and when the 1906 earthquake left her reinforced-concrete Mills College campanile standing amid the rubble, the commissions never stopped: over 700 buildings in a five-decade practice, including a long run of YWCAs, women's clubs and campus buildings for clients other architects didn't court. William Randolph Hearst kept her occupied for nearly thirty years at San Simeon, where she managed everything from Roman pools to the zoo's bear grottos while running her San Francisco office by overnight train. She gave no interviews, published nothing, and burned most of her papers, believing buildings should speak for themselves. The AIA finally awarded her its Gold Medal in 2014, its first to a woman, fifty-seven years after her death.

projects.title: Hearst Castle
projects.blurb: La Cuesta Encantada: a Mediterranean hilltop compound assembled over decades around Hearst's insatiable collecting, Roman and Neptune pools included.

projects.title: Asilomar Conference Grounds
projects.blurb: A YWCA retreat of redwood and stone Arts and Crafts lodges among the Monterey dunes; sixteen Morgan buildings survive.

projects.title: Berkeley City Club
projects.blurb: A six-story Moorish-Gothic women's club in reinforced concrete, its vaulted indoor pool nicknamed the little castle's crown jewel by members.

projects.title: El Campanil, Mills College
projects.blurb: A 72-foot reinforced-concrete bell tower that rode out the 1906 earthquake untouched and made her reputation.

projects.title: Chapel of the Chimes
projects.blurb: A columbarium of cloistered courts, fountains and filtered light — one of the least morbid buildings for the dead in America.

projects.title: Herald Examiner Building
projects.blurb: Mission Revival headquarters for Hearst's Los Angeles paper, her first big commission for him.

projects.title: Wyntoon
projects.blurb: Hearst's forest estate rebuilt as a Bavarian fairy-tale village on the McCloud, murals and all.

projects.title: St. John's Presbyterian Church
projects.blurb: Exposed redwood framing as the whole architecture; a Bay Region landmark now serving as a playhouse.

projects.title: Fairmont Hotel Restoration
projects.blurb: The fire-gutted hotel reopened exactly one year after the earthquake, with Morgan the engineer-architect who made it stand.

projects.title: Hearst Memorial Gymnasium
projects.blurb: A Beaux-Arts women's gymnasium for the Berkeley campus, designed with Bernard Maybeck, pools framed by urns.

name: Eliel Saarinen
bio: Saarinen had two full careers separated by an ocean and a second-place prize. In Finland, with Gesellius and Lindgren, he built the granite National Romanticism of a country rehearsing its independence — the Paris 1900 pavilion, the National Museum, and Helsinki's great station, whose stone giants holding lamps are as close as railway architecture gets to myth; the three partners lived and worked together at Hvitträsk, the forest studio-home they built themselves. His 1922 Chicago Tribune entry finished second but out-influenced the winner, its telescoping setbacks becoming the template for a decade of American skyscrapers, and it carried him to the United States at forty-nine. There George Booth handed him Cranbrook, which he planned, built and ran as the Academy's president, teaching a generation that included Eames, Bertoia and his own son Eero. He died at Cranbrook in 1950, a founding father twice over.

projects.title: Helsinki Central Station
projects.blurb: Granite arch, clock tower and two pairs of colossal lantern-bearers; National Romanticism rationalized into one of the world's great stations.

projects.title: Cranbrook Campus
projects.blurb: Schools, academy, museum and his own house, built and directed over two decades — a total work of art that doubled as America's Bauhaus.

projects.title: Chicago Tribune Competition Entry
projects.blurb: Second prize, first influence: the stepped-back tower that Louis Sullivan praised over the winner and American cities built for a decade.

projects.title: Hvitträsk
projects.blurb: The lakeside log-and-stone compound where the three partners lived, worked and feuded; now a museum.

projects.title: National Museum of Finland
projects.blurb: A national history museum composed as a granite medley of Finnish church and castle forms.

projects.title: First Christian Church
projects.blurb: A brick box and freestanding campanile that count among the first modernist churches in America, in the town Eero and others would fill after him.

projects.title: Kleinhans Music Hall
projects.blurb: A curved-shell concert hall of exceptional acoustics, designed with Eero as the practice became father-and-son.

projects.title: Christ Church Lutheran
projects.blurb: His last completed building: plain brick, side-lit chancel, not an ounce of rhetoric — modern religious space at its quietest.

projects.title: Crow Island School
projects.blurb: With Eero and Perkins & Will: the child-scaled, single-story elementary school that became the postwar American template.

projects.title: Finnish Pavilion, Paris 1900
projects.blurb: The exposition pavilion that announced both the young partnership and, diplomatically speaking, Finland itself.
